qs.q: An investigator studies an enzyme-catalyzed reaction and observes that maximum velocity increases when an activator molecule binds to a non-active site. What type of allosteric regulation is occurring?
o: K system allosteric activation altering substrate affinity without changing Vmax
V system allosteric activation increasing catalytic turnover rate parameters
Covalent modification phosphorylation enhancing intrinsic enzymatic activity
Feedback inhibition slowing down upstream metabolic pathway production rates
Zymogen cleavage exposing hidden catalytic pockets for substrate binding
qs.e: In V-system allosteric enzymes, the activator increases Vmax without necessarily affecting the apparent Km.

qs.q: Allosteric regulation of an enzyme typically involves:
o: D. Enzyme amount changes via synthesis or degradation
C. Molecule occupies the active site, blocking substrate entry
B. Enzyme undergoes covalent modification such as phosphorylation
A. Effector binds away from the active site, altering enzyme shape
qs.e: Allosteric regulation involves the binding of an effector molecule to an allosteric site (a site distinct from the active site) on the enzyme. This binding induces a conformational change that affects the enzyme's activity, either activating or inhibiting it.

ai.title: Allosteric Regulation
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Allosteric regulation controls enzyme activity by binding molecules at sites other than the active site, inducing conformational changes that enhance or inhibit function. Clinically, this mechanism underlies drug action, metabolic disorders, and pathogen resistance.

b: Effectors can be activators or inhibitors
sections.p: Allosteric sites are distinct from catalytic sites; binding of an effector changes enzyme shape, affecting substrate affinity or catalytic rate. This allows rapid, reversible control of metabolic pathways.

b: R state: high affinity, high activity
T state: low affinity, low activity
sections.p: Effectors bind to allosteric sites, stabilising either an active (R) or inactive (T) conformation. The equilibrium shifts depending on effector concentration, temperature, and pH.
Allosteric regulation integrates cellular signals: ATP, ADP, citrate, and hormones. It provides feedback inhibition or activation, ensuring metabolic flux matches demand.

b: Glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe) – defective allosteric regulation of glycogen phosphorylase
sections.p: Mutations that alter allosteric sites can lock enzymes in active or inactive states, leading to metabolic diseases. Overactive enzymes may cause hypermetabolism; underactive enzymes can cause accumulation of substrates.

b: Allopurinol – inhibits xanthine oxidase allosterically, reducing uric acid
sections.p: Understanding allosteric sites guides drug design: allosteric inhibitors (e.g., allopurinol) and activators (e.g., statin co‑activators). In low‑resource settings, monitoring metabolic markers (e.g., lactate, ammonia) helps detect dysregulation.

b: Allosteric inhibitors are often safer due to lower risk of complete enzyme blockade
sections.p: Remember that allosteric regulation is reversible and often cooperative. In exams, focus on the effect of effector concentration, the R/T equilibrium, and clinical examples of dysregulation.

b: Competitive inhibition – binds active site, reversible
sections.p: Allosteric regulation is distinct from competitive inhibition, which binds the active site. It is also different from covalent modification (phosphorylation).

b: Genetic variants may require higher effector concentrations for activation
sections.p: Low enzyme activity in vitro may not reflect in vivo allosteric activation; genetic polymorphisms can alter effector sensitivity.

b: Provide glucose in hypoglycaemia due to impaired glycogenolysis
sections.p: Treat underlying metabolic disorder, provide supportive care, and use specific allosteric modulators when available. Monitor metabolic panels and adjust therapy based on response.
Severe metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, or unexplained organ failure warrant urgent referral.
